      <title>California’s coastal communities on alert as biggest waves in years hit state</title>
      <link>https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026/nov/20/california-coastal-communities-alert-big-waves-hit-state</link>
      <description><p>Hazard warnings issued throughout week after powerful swells and waves of more than 9 metres recorded</p><p>Multiple coastal hazard warnings were issued this week across California as successive areas of low pressure generated powerful swells and large breaking waves for coastal communities. Beaches and piers were closed last weekend as large waves crashed into California’s coastline. Offshore National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration buoys recorded wave heights of greater than 30ft (9 metres) last Friday. The Monterey, California, buoy recorded a wave height of 34.1ft, which would make it the highest reading in 30 years.</p><p>Coastal warnings extended from last weekend through this week, with alerts extending until Friday night. Waves of 10-18ft are expected, with local sets of 18-22ft for San Luis Obispo county beaches and Santa Barbara county central coast beaches. These Pacific storm systems are also bringing unsettled conditions across the western US, with heavy rain, mountain snow, and strong winds through the coming days. Already, record-breaking rainfall affected San Fransisco on Wednesday, with heavy rain also causing 32,000 customers to lose power in Sacramento. Into this weekend, a further area of low pressure will bring considerable amounts of moisture for southern Oregon and northern California. By Sunday night, more than 100mm (4in) of rain is expected in places, with further snowfall for areas such as Donner Pass across the northern Sierra Nevada mountains.</p> <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026/nov/20/california-coastal-communities-alert-big-waves-hit-state">Continue reading...</a></description>

      <description><p>The trees, intended for an unnamed buyer in Georgia, were reportedly dug up without the necessary permits</p><p>Environmentalists in South Africa are racing to replant five centuries-old baobabs after the 20-tonne trees were dug up by an exporter, who tried to ship them thousands of miles to Georgia.</p><p>The baobabs arrived at a reserve in Timbavati, in north-eastern South Africa, on Wednesday, where they will be replanted and supported by cables to help them recover.       <link>https://www.theguardian.com/global-development/2026/nov/19/women-girls-rights-rape-sexual-violence-africa-marriage-unfpa</link>
      <description><p>Almost half of women in west and central Africa cannot withhold consent, with girls worst affected, UNFPA finds</p><p>One in four women around the world have no power of consent if their husband or partner demands sex, according to a UN report.</p><p>In west and central Africa, almost half of women (45%) are not able to say no in their own marriage, while a third of women (33%) in east and southern Africa and in Arab states face the same predicament.       <link>https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/nov/18/us-sanctions-icj-judges-myanmar-genocide-ruling-israel-gaza-court</link>
      <description><p>A ruling against Myanmar could set precedent for court’s judgment on Israel’s actions in Gaza</p><p>Fears are growing that the US could impose sanctions on judges at the international court of justice, including this year’s <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/oct/09/navanethem-navi-pillay-wins-nobel-peace-prize">Nobel peace prize winner, Navi Pillay</a>, if the <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/nov/15/myanmar-rohingya-genocide-icj">court rules on Thursday that the Myanmar government committed genocide</a> against the Rohingya.</p><p>The ICJ has never found a state responsible for committing genocide, and a significant factor in previous cases has been how to prove “intent” in a crime defined as acts committed with the “intent to destroy, in whole or in part” a national, ethnical, racial or religious group.</p> <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/nov/18/us-sanctions-icj-judges-myanmar-genocide-ruling-israel-gaza-court">Continue reading...</a></description>

      <title>European Commission accused of sugarcoating figures to release funds to Egypt</title>
      <link>https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/nov/18/european-commission-accused-sugarcoating-figures-egypt-loans</link>
      <description><p>Leaked documents raise questions about claims Egypt met welfare targets to qualify for €2.5bn in loans</p><p>The European Commission has been accused of sugarcoating figures to enable it to release funds to Egypt under a landmark pact with the authoritarian government of Abdel Fatah al-Sisi.</p><p>The charge relates to a €7.4bn deal <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/world/2024/mar/17/egypt-eu-deal-refugees-mediterranean">promised by Ursula von der Leyen</a>, the European Commission president, to al-Sisi on a high-profile visit to Cairo in 2024. The three-year “strategic and comprehensive partnership” was intended to bolster Egypt’s shaky economy, deter migrants from coming to Europe and shore up a region reeling from the 7 October attacks and Israel’s war on Gaza.</p> <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/nov/18/european-commission-accused-sugarcoating-figures-egypt-loans">Continue reading...</a></description>

On Nov. 20, 1998, the first piece of the International Space Station launched into orbit.

The 42,000-pound module is called Zarya, and it's about the size of a tour bus. Zarya launched on board a Russian Proton rocket. Two weeks later, NASA's STS-88 shuttle mission aboard Endeavour brought the Unity module into space. The STS-88 astronauts connected the two modules in orbit.

Zarya was built by the Russians, but it was paid for by the United States. NASA contracted a Russian company to build it for half the price of what the American company Lockheed Martin would have charged. These days, Zarya is mainly used for storage and for external fuel tanks. The module also has docking ports for Russian Progress cargo ships and Soyuz spacecraft that carry crews to and from the space station.

Today, the International Space Station is about the size of a football field and typically hosts up to seven crewmembers. But back in 1998, it was a pretty tight squeeze.

Why it mattered

As of this writing, the International Space Station is 28 years old, and has seen steady rotating crews of astronauts since the year 2000 (for 26 years and counting). It is a marvel of space engineering, but every engineering marvel begins the same: with the first piece.

And that is what the Zarya module is: The foundation of the International Space Station.

Zarya, also known as the Functional Cargo Block (or Russian acronym FGB), is the core module of the space station around which every other module was attached. It weighed 42,600 pounds at launch and is just aver 41 feet long and 13.5 feet wide. Inside, it boasts a total habitable volume of 1,650 cubic feet.

NASA paid $220 million for Zarya's construction at the Krunichev State Research and Production Space Center in Moscow, with work beginning in 1994 and ending in 1998. The module is a central hub based on the success of Russia's Salyut space station designs, with two solar arrays for power and 16 external tanks to store propellant.

While NASA's space shuttle Endeavour was the first to meet Zarya (and attach NASA's core Unity connecting module to it), it wasn't until Russia'z Zvezda service launched in 2000 and docked with Zarya's aft that the fledgling space station was large enough to accomodate its first three-person crew, Expedition 1.

Over the last 28 years, giant backbone-like metal trusses, solar wings and many other modules (built by Russia, NASA, Europe, Canada and Japan) have greatly expanded the living area of the station. Many ISS components could not be tested with one another on the ground, meaning the first time they were attached was in space during construction.

The result is a feat of space construction that has only recently seen a rival as China works to expand its own Tiangong space station.

]]> <![CDATA[ Don't turn the moon into the Wild West, scientists warn ]]> Researchers are calling for a moratorium on industrial exploitation of the moon, fearing that rapid development could cause irreversible environmental damage and destroy invaluable scientific material.

Both China and the U.S. are pushing forward with plans to establish permanent human settlements on the moon by the end of the next decade. Commercial players want to build businesses supporting these future explorers by mining for resources such as water, construction materials, industrial metals and rare earth minerals.

However, some scientists argue that a temporary ban on lunar industrialization is necessary to allow regulations to catch up and limit what can be allowed in order to prevent a moon rush from destroying the pristine lunar environment.

Two such researchers are Florian Rabitz, a professor of climate and technology governance at Vilnius University in Lithuania, and Xiao-Shan Yap, an assistant professor of Earth-space sustainability at Utrecht University in the Netherlands. In a piece published last month in the journal Global Environmental Politics, the pair call for "robust international regulations" and "broad and inclusive deliberation" to allow the global community to carefully consider the impact of economic activities on the moon.

In addition to the threat to the scientifically priceless lunar landscape, the researchers also object to the colonization of the moon by a small number of powerful players — namely China, the U.S. and their respective close allies.

"With the moon it's absolutely clear that whoever is doing the big infrastructure work is going to be asserting their position, including by defining their own exclusive territories," Rabitz said in a statement. "That shouldn't be the Wild West."

Rabitz pointed out that, although the United Nations' 1967 Outer Space Treaty prevents individual nations from appropriating the moon, Earth's natural satellite and its valuable resources are unlikely to remain truly neutral territory if its exploitation is going to be led by a small number of powerful nations.

]]> <![CDATA[ GTA hasn't gone to space (yet), but these sci-fi games can offer you a life of crime among the stars ]]> GTA 6 has only just come out, and it's already taken the world by storm and positioned itself as one of the greatest games of all time. Great news for gamers, but what about sci-fi fans?

To this day, Rockstar Games sadly hasn't embraced sci-fi with any of its open-world games (save for those UFO Easter eggs). It doesn't seem likely they'll journey to the stars anytime soon — you can't really do cutting societal satire about space — but that doesn't mean there aren't GTA-adjacent sci-fi adventures set in outer space.

The frustrating thing is that no one has exactly cracked that pitch yet. Non-linear games set in outer space tend to be either too ambitious, like No Man's Sky, or too focused on specific experiences like space combat, like Star Wars: Squadrons.

The end result is a roster of great sandboxes that let us journey to different star systems, but no game that dares to explore a criminal fantasy with the level of depth and opportunities seen in the last few Rockstar games.

With new hardware powering far more complex open-world games, it's only a matter of time before "GTA in space" is a real thing. For now, there are some space games that let us explore sci-fi worlds, roleplaying as criminals and outlaws amongst the stars.

Roleplaying a space outlaw

Massive space RPGs like Starfield and The Outer Worlds 2 offer vast playgrounds you can explore and redefine through your actions. The lawful path is the obvious choice if you'd like to save the galaxy, but a life of crime awaits those who tire of the heroics.

Starfield even has a "new game plus" mechanic baked into the player's journey, encouraging experimentation and living different lives, so if you stick with the divisive space RPG, the criminal life is all but unavoidable. And in traditional Bethesda fashion, you're not rushed to the next "main" objective, so if you want to become the most dangerous space criminal in the Settled Systems, you'll be supported by the mechanics and systems. You can always get back to saving the galaxy when you feel like it.

The Outer Worlds 2 is another option if you want to become a star-surfing scoundrel. It might not be as absurdly expansive as Starfield, but Obsidian's whole deal has always been freedom of choice and roleplaying, so you can bet this humorous sequel also lets the protagonist become a bit of an a-hole. The main story already sets you in a collision course with corporate interests, too. Like in Mass Effect and other classic space RPGs, it's your choice to be either a goody-two-shoes or an edgy maniac, and I won't lie: the second option is usually more entertaining.

Last but not least, there's a third game that also has enough going on to support a GTA-inspired fantasy in outer space: No Man's Sky.

It's grown so much over the years that its original space exploration premise has been buried by content like fully customizable space stations, actual cities and towns with alien NPCs, gigantic kaiju-like beasts, and... fishing. The endless free updates have pushed the roleplaying aspects deeper, as Hello Games are really making it the "forever" space game.

Most importantly though, you can be the greatest bad guy the virtually infinite universe has ever seen, controlling entire pirate fleets and firing on (or stealing) every spaceship that you come across. It might be a bit aimless for some, but if you love a "forever game" then NMS can be the biggest space-set criminal sim ever created.

Star Wars almost got it right

Though it took too long, Star Wars has gotten really close to cracking the GTA formula in outer space in a shameless enough way. 2024's Star Wars Outlaws is, to this date, the closest thing we've received to a space-set sandbox directly inspired by Rockstar's huge hits.

By letting us fully embrace the Han Solo-like scoundrel fantasy, Massive Entertainment delivered a Star Wars adventure that's all about breaking the law. Hell, they even got a wanted system in there that has protagonist Kay Vess dodging stormtroopers and rival criminal factions like you would in Vice City.

Star Wars Outlaws' take on GTA isn't just about the surface-level gameplay and open structure; it also understands much of its playful tone, moral ambiguity, and stressful rhythm. Jumping between several medium-sized maps set on different planets and spaceship sections breaks up the experience a little, so it never quite reaches that level of seamless immersion, but if anyone wants to do a focused version of GTA in space in the future, Massive's attempt is the one game that got at least halfway there.

The ones we lost

Before we go (and before you go back to playing GTA VI), we should remember the daring video games that, for a variety of reasons, never got to realize their visions of a crime-oriented space adventure.

Remember Star Wars 1313 and Visceral Games' cancelled project? It's hard not to spot some of their DNA surviving in Outlaws. As Luke Skywalker wisely said before noping out, "No one's ever really gone." Lucasfilm loves that, and it extends to binned video games too, thankfully. Even the elusive Battlefront 3 is back from the dead now.

Bethesda also had something going at some point with "Prey 2", a bounty hunter action game set in a cyberpunk-ish alien world. Before it was canned, it dropped one of the coolest CG game trailers ever made and teased us with a Blade Runner-esque future long before Cyberpunk hit our consoles.

Looking at the future, Ubisoft's Beyond Good & Evil 2 wants to go big and lawless, potentially iterating on Star Wars Outlaws and other open-world crime sims. But years after its announcement and many mind-boggling development news updates, it's hard to believe it's really ever coming out. Maybe the "Before GTA VI" meme can morph into "Before BG&E2" now that Rockstar's masterpiece is finally out.

Ultimately, Rockstar is Rockstar. A one-of-a-kind megastudio with nearly unlimited resources. Trying to replicate GTA does — either on Earth or among the stars — would be an Icarus flight in the making for most studios. There are some GTA-flavored space adventures out there, as we've shown, but we're still waiting for the one. Something that matches the deep storytelling, complete freedom, and cheeky tone of Rockstar's iconic series.

OK, I gotta get out of here, I'm too hip for this, I gotta play GTA VI some more.

]]> <![CDATA[ There's an impostor hiding in the Hyades star cluster. Can you spot it? ]]> For years I looked at Taurus and saw something perfectly sensible. There was the Hyades, the big V-shaped cluster that forms the bull's face, with Aldebaran, noticeably brighter and more orange than the other stars, the dominant star. Every diagram reinforced the arrangement — Aldebaran was the eye of Taurus, the Hyades made the face, and in my head they became one object.

Then I discovered that Aldebaran has nothing to do with the Hyades. I remember going outside afterward and looking again, half expecting the deception to become obvious now that I knew. It didn't. Aldebaran still looked completely at home among the other stars. The difference is hidden in the one dimension our eyes judge poorly when we look into space — depth. Aldebaran is about 65 light-years away, while the Hyades are roughly 150 light-years distant. The orange eye of Taurus is a foreground star that happens to lie almost exactly along our line of sight toward the Hyades.

This fact exposes one of the most convincing tricks in stargazing. The night sky looks flat, and our brains are extremely willing to believe it. But it has incredible depth — and when you can see parts of the night sky in 3D, that's when you begin to appreciate that you're not looking at a flat map. Instead, you begin to see our cosmic neighborhood as it really is. By appreciating depth, you learn its geography.

What's happening and when to look

Taurus is now easy to find from the Northern Hemisphere during the evening. Once it's dark, look east for a small, tight knot of stars — the Pleiades open cluster (M45) — and then look nearby for a much larger V-shaped arrangement. That V is the Hyades, with unmistakably orange Aldebaran apparently sitting on one arm. Aldebaran's name is derived from the Arabic Al Dabarān, meaning "the follower," because it appears to trail the Pleiades across the night sky.

The Hyades is a real physical group of stars — an open cluster — that formed together and moves through our galaxy together. About 153 light-years away, the Hyades is the nearest open star cluster to Earth. The name means "the rainmakers" because their rising and setting times in the ancient Greek sky coincided with wet weather. The stars in the Hyades are of a similar age — and mostly sun-like stars, or similar — so astronomers can tell that they all formed together in the same nebula.

Orange-red star Aldebaran — the 14th-brightest star in the night sky — is the interloper, sitting less than half as far away from the sun. If you could somehow view the neighborhood from another part of the Milky Way, the familiar arrangement would fall apart. Aldebaran would no longer sit conveniently in the bull's face, and Taurus itself would stop looking like a bull.

Constellations aren't objects in the same sense as a planet or star cluster. They are merely views. Even stars that appear almost side by side can be separated by enormous distances. Our entire view of the night sky is a line-of-sight, 2D phenomenon — so all the patterns we see are an illusion.

How and when I'm watching it

Start with Aldebaran and the Hyades using only unaided eyes. Once you have the V, remind yourself of the distances — roughly 65 light-years for Aldebaran and 150 for the Hyades — and try to imagine pulling the orange star toward you while leaving the rest of the cluster behind. Stargazing like this can be much harder than it sounds. Even the brains of seasoned stargazers are hard-wired to find patterns of stars — constellations — and they rarely practice seeing stars at their correct distances.

Binoculars are worth using for the Hyades because the cluster is broad, so low magnification suits it well. Binoculars show many additional stars, but that's not really the point. Knowing what you're looking at changes the observation more than magnification does.

Trying to see the night sky in 3D is best done one constellation at a time, but I warn you — it makes you suspicious of everything. Next time you trace Orion, Cassiopeia or Auriga, you'll always be wondering which stars are nearby and which merely look that way. Looking up the distances and working it all out for yourself is an eye-opening experience.

Learning constellations gets you around the sky in a basic sense, but learning how to dismantle them and put them back together is when you begin to know the night sky as it really is.

Stargazer's corner: November 20-26, 2026

This week is dominated by the moon. The moon is already waxing when the week begins and becomes the full Beaver Moon — a supermoon — on Nov. 24. That means progressively brighter evening skies and increasingly poor conditions for faint galaxies, nebulae and other low-contrast objects. Aldebaran and the main Hyades stars are bright enough to see from suburban skies even under strong moonlight, so you don't need to travel somewhere properly dark. Swapping your view from 2D to 3D takes only a little imagination. However, that could change in the few nights around the full moon — particularly on Nov. 23, when the waxing gibbous moon will move close to the nearby Pleiades, its strong light reducing the number of faint stars visible around them. Use binoculars to find some of its hundreds of stars.

Constellation of the week: Cepheus

I'm a stargazer and not at all interested in Greek mythology, but it sometimes helps to know a few basic ancient myths when finding constellations. A good example is the constellation Cepheus. It's named after a king of Ethiopia, husband of Cassiopeia and father of Andromeda — all three of which are close by in the northern sky right now. Look west after dark, away from the bright moon, to find the Summer Triangle — Vega, Deneb and Altair — which by now is sinking into the west. From Deneb, look north for a distinctive five-star pattern resembling a child's drawing of a house, with a square base and pointed roof. That's Cepheus. Its brightest star is Alderamin, about 49 light-years away, which marks one corner of the "house."

]]> <![CDATA[ Could an ancient solar eclipse rewrite Egyptian history? ]]> The solar system is a clock that can be run in both directions. On Aug. 2, 2027, that clock will bring the moon's dark central shadow — a path of totality — back to Egypt. A total solar eclipse will sweep across the country, passing directly over Luxor and plunging some of ancient Egypt's greatest surviving monuments into darkness. Totality will begin in Luxor at approximately 1:02 p.m. EEST and last 6 minutes 22 seconds, according to Time and Date.

We know when it will happen because we can calculate the motions of Earth and the moon centuries in advance. But run the same celestial clock backward and eclipses become one of nature's most precise timestamps.

Astronomers can reconstruct where the moon's shadow fell thousands of years ago, even when nobody left a record of it. When an ancient text reliably describes an eclipse, it can anchor a moment in history to a specific place and time.

Did an eclipse rewrite the Pyramid Age?

We know from astronomical calculations that eclipses crossed Egypt long before anyone left an identifiable written record of one. On April 1, 2471 B.C., a total solar eclipse swept across northern Egypt during the age of the great pyramid builders. In research published in 2025, archaeoastronomer Giulio Magli at the Polytechnic University of Milan proposed that the eclipse may help explain why Pharaoh Shepseskaf broke with tradition and built a huge rectangular tomb at South Saqqara instead of a pyramid. It's a tantalizing hypothesis, but no surviving Egyptian text records the eclipse.

Astronomers can calculate that an eclipse happened, but using it as a historical timestamp requires evidence that someone actually saw it and recorded it. That's where an eclipse almost 1,300 years later becomes particularly intriguing.

Is the oldest recorded eclipse hidden in the Bible?

A passage in the Old Testament book of Joshua describes the sun and moon as if they stopped in the sky. After leading the people of Israel into Canaan — modern-day Israel and Palestine — Joshua prayed: "Sun, stand still at Gibeon, and moon, in the Valley of Aijalon. And the sun stood still, and the moon stopped, until the nation took vengeance on their enemies." Ancient Gibeon is about six miles (10 kilometers) northwest of Jerusalem.

In research published in 2017, researchers Colin Humphreys and Graeme Waddington at Cambridge University in the U.K. claimed it could refer to an annular solar eclipse on Oct. 30, 1207 B.C. It's a controversial interpretation, not least because it depends on exactly how the ancient Hebrew text is translated. However, if correct, it could be the oldest recorded solar eclipse with a date that has been identified — and it could also more accurately date the reign of Ramesses II. Also known as Ramesses the Great, he reigned for 66 years during Egypt's New Kingdom, commissioned Abu Simbel, made major additions to Karnak and Luxor Temple, and lived to be over 90. His reign marked the final peak of ancient Egyptian imperial power. According to the BBC, he is the "Jupiter" of the pharaonic system. However, the precise dates of his reign remain subject to debate, with historians using a combination of archaeological, historical and astronomical evidence to reconstruct the chronology.

The riddle of the Merneptah Stele

Now in the Egyptian Museum in Cairo, the Merneptah Stele is a large inscribed granite monument written in the fifth year of Pharaoh Merneptah's reign, successor to Ramesses II. Discovered in 1896 at Merneptah's mortuary temple on the west bank of the Nile, opposite modern-day Luxor, it describes an Egyptian military campaign in Canaan and mentions Israelites. Egyptologists generally date Merneptah's reign to around 1213 — 1203 B.C., placing his fifth year around 1209/1208 B.C. That means the Israelites were already living in Canaan by then.

Using calculations that accounted for changes in Earth's rotation over thousands of years, Humphreys and Waddington identified an annular eclipse visible from Canaan for five minutes on the afternoon of Oct. 30, 1207 B.C. If the biblical passage does describe this event, that's a fixed astronomical date that could be used to refine the chronology of the Egyptian pharaohs. The researchers proposed that it occurred during the second, third or fourth year of Merneptah's reign.

Can an eclipse rewrite history?

If Humphreys and Waddington's interpretation of the biblical text is correct, the eclipse of 1207 B.C. could be the oldest solar eclipse identified in a written record. The researchers propose that Ramesses II reigned from approximately 1276 to 1210, with an uncertainty of about a year, slightly different from the conventional dates of 1279-1213 B.C. used by the British Museum.

So an eclipse can be like a timestamp on an undated photograph, but this one does not show that the book of Joshua actually describes an eclipse. The interpretation of the Hebrew has been challenged by Marinus Anthony van der Sluijs, whose paper argues that the biblical narrative states that the sun was standing over Gibeon and the moon was over the Valley of Aijalon simultaneously — so not an eclipse at all.

On Aug. 2, 2027, there will be no such ambiguity. We already know where the moon's shadow will cross Egypt, when it will reach Luxor and how long darkness will last. Almost 4,500 years separate that eclipse from the one that crossed Egypt in 2471 B.C. and 3,233 years from 1207 B.C., but both are movements of the same celestial clock. Run it forwards, and it predicts the future. Run it backward, and occasionally an eclipse of the sun can put a date on history.

A major item dealt with by the DIA is "counterspace" — and it's not the kind that you'll find in your kitchen.

Counterspace operations can be either offensive or defensive. They can be used on purpose to reversibly or irreversibly deny, disrupt, degrade, damage or destroy a space object or component of a space system.

Here are the key elements of counterspace, as identified within the DIA report:

  • Antisatellite (ASAT) missiles are designed to kinetically strike and destroy satellites. ASAT missiles could produce massive amounts of debris that can remain in orbit for decades or even centuries.
  • Physical or cyberattacks against ground sites and other terrestrial infrastructure supporting space operations can also threaten satellite services. Cyber counterspace attacks target the satellite data within the transmission signal, along with the systems that use, transmit and control the flow of data.
  • Electronic attacks include jamming and spoofing techniques to target a nation's use of the electromagnetic spectrum. Electronic attacks can interfere with systems used for communications and command and control of military forces, including piloted and unpiloted vehicles.

The Himalayas tower below the clouds, capped in icy snow in new snapshots captured from aboard the International Space Station.

Canadian Space Agency astronaut Joshua Kutryk was looking out one of the windows aboard the space station when the most incredible view came into focus  — and thankfully he had a camera handy and was able to capture these striking scenes of the Himalayas from space.

Above the mountain range, fluffy clouds hang in the atmosphere. Below, the expansive Himalayas are covered in bright snow and ice, which looks somehow both white and blue at the same time as the bright sunlight streaks across the breathtaking expanse.

This frosty winter scene showcases the mountain range from orbit, from about 250 miles (400 kilometers) above Earth's surface. But even from this distance, the magnitude of this mountain range is palpable. The Himalayas stretch across five different countries including Nepal, India, China, Bhutan and Pakistan. And the Himalayas include some of the highest mountain peaks on planet Earth, including Mount Everest.

Why is it incredible?

From orbit around Earth, you might expect even the largest landmarks on our planet to appear miniscule. But somehow, in these photographs snapped by Kutryk during NASA's SpaceX Crew-13 mission, even from hundreds of miles above our planet you can really see and feel the immense scale of this mammoth mountain range.

It's unclear exactly where above the mountain range these photographs were taken, but it is always amazing to think that within these sweeping landscapes are people living their lives, likely unaware that an astronaut is taking in the beauty of their home.

Perhaps somewhere hidden under the clouds in one of Kutryk's photographs are hikers climbing up the side of Mt. Everest, completing their own bucket list adventure as the astronauts watching from above complete theirs.

]]> <![CDATA[ I got to tour SpaceX's Starfactory facility in Starbase, Texas, and what I saw blew my mind ]]> STARBASE, Texas  — I just finished covering the Starship Flight 15 mission, and SpaceXs incredible launch tower catch of the returned Ship 42 spacecraft isn't the only thing over the weekend that left me speechless.

The morning of the launch (Nov. 13), SpaceX invited media on a tour of Starbase's Starfactory facility, where it manufactures and assembles both stages of its massive Starship rocket - an unprecedented behind-the-scenes look at the production and scale of SpaceX's operations, and a glimpse of things to come as Starship notches more and more milestones the more it flies.

For some context, the five-story-tall Starfactory spans approximately 1 million square feet (~93,000 meters), with operations split between Starship's Super Heavy boosters and upper stage Ships, and nearly 330,000 additional square feet (30,000 square meters) of office space. SpaceX officials describe its design as one more akin to an automotive manufacturing plant than that of a typical aerospace production site, and inside, it is absolutely alive with activity.

Inside Starfactory

We entered through an arch-covered doorway underneath the giant "X" sign on the building's shorter face. Our media gaggle was met with curious glances as we were shown through the doors and guided onto the factory floor - few are ever able to cross that threshold outside of SpaceX employees, and our presence seemed as novel to those busy working as it was to us.

Inside, we were struck with the sheer enormity of Starship's scale. Giant stainless-steel rocket parts were meticulously scattered across different subassembly stations throughout the building, with Ship nose cones, cylindrical sections and booster components all under various stages of manufacture. The sheer quantity of the hardware was staggering, and being so close to each as we walked Starfactory's throughways was an eye-opener.

Starbase is a unique partnership of privately-owned SpaceX property and publicly-accessible land and shoreline, which has created the unique ability for anyone with a mind to do so to drive right up to the the Starship launch pad to see the facilities up close (within a few hundred feet or so, which, as rockets go, is very, very close).

Fully stacked, Starship stands more than 400 feet (120 meters) tall. Standing next to such a towering colossus on the pad is enough to drive home just how big the launch vehicle is, but standing next its segmented components inside Starfactory is even more humbling; like seeing one of Ship's upper aerodynamic flaps, which are each large enough when laid flat that you could park a pair of large SUVs on their faces with room to spare.

As our tour continued and we passed rows of nose cones under preparation for integration, numbering as high as Ship 51, one stood out from the others. In the distance, only visible for moment between the overlapping views of other Ships as we walked through the production stations, was a nose cone with a series of windows cut out of its face - undoubtedly a prototype for, or possibly even the final article that will be used as NASA's Artemis lunar lander.

NASA has contracted SpaceX to develop a version of Starship capable of landing astronauts on the moon as a part of the agency's Artemis program, and this appeared to the Ship being readied for when that mission arrives. NASA is targeting Artemis IV as the program's first crewed lunar landing in 2028, and while the decision solidifying Starship as the lander tasked with that mission isn't finalized (Blue Origin is also vying for that spot with its Blue Moon lander), SpaceX is clearly operating with the intention of coming out ahead.

But Artemis is clearly not SpaceX's only focus, as evident by the many, many other Ships in production that did not have window holes carved out of them.SpaceX officials said the company is currently completing about one Ship upper stage every two weeks, and one Super Heavy booster every four weeks, with overlapping production allowing multiple rockets to move through the factory simultaneously. The majority of the vehicles currently being assembled will carry stacks of SpaceX's upgraded Starlink Version 3 (V3) satellites.

The company's Starlink network in low Earth orbit currently consists of more than 11,000 spacecraft beaming wireless internet to SpaceX customers across the globe. All of those were launched on SpaceX's workhorse Falcon 9 rocket, with the exception of a few more than 50 delivered on Starship's two most recent test flights. Both carried V3 Starlink stacks to add to the constellation, which SpaceX officials say each added the data capacity equivalent to ten Falcon 9 Starlink launches. And, as they fine tune Starship's design, SpaceX plans to increase the vehicle's launch cadence dramatically, growing the Starlink network as it does.

SpaceX CEO Elon Musk has stated the company hopes to launch Starship about once a week beginning in 2027, and with the number of Ships we saw lined up inside Starfactory, launch vehicle inventory doesn't seem like it will be to blame if that goal isn't realized.

Building rockets like cars (and Lego bricks)

SpaceX has adopted a manufacturing process modeled after the automotive industry, where efficiency and reproduction allow for the manufacture of large numbers of identical parts. Automation is a critical part of that process, but not one SpaceX is ready to entirely rely on.

Much of the equipment and tools being used for Starship's production were designed by SpaceX engineers, who are constantly refining production processes to eliminate bottlenecks. And SpaceX has deliberately kept technicians on the floor as Starship's design continues to evolve, rather than automating procedures that might soon become obsolete.

Our tour guide compared SpaceX's manufacturing consistency goals to that of Lego bricks, which are famously precise in their production down to the micro-millimeter accuracy of what now number more than 1 trillion bricks made since the toy company began in the 1940s.

Expansion

Exiting the far side of the building, we stood in the shadow of SpaceX's two towering Mega Bays, where the sections of Starship are stacked and integrated with their engines - there's one hanger for Ship, and another for Super Heavy. Each can hold about five or six assemblies, and housed two or three vehicles at the time our tour was brought by.

Both Mega Bays, however, looked small against the adjacent Gigabay SpaceX is currently constructing. At approximately 700,000 square feet (65,000 square meters), Gigabay will be equipped with room to accommodate up to 24 vehicles at a time, and will facilitate a major increase in SpaceX's ability to assemble its Ship and Super Heavy rockets.

Part of SpaceX's goal with Starship is to make all of what we got to see completely routine; to make rocket launches and landings as ordinary as commercial airline flights. Still, standing inside Starfactory, surrounded on all sides by huge spacecraft in various stages of assembly, it was hard to imagine a reality where giant rockets flying to and from space on a regular basis wouldn't feel like science fiction.

Later that day a giant rocket launched to outer space - Super Heavy did attempt a return to pad, but was diverted for an offshore landing instead, where it exploded. But the next day, Ship 42 came plunging through the overcast cloud cover, falling belly-first toward the same tower it left just a couple dozen hours before. And then it lit its engines and was caught by the tower.

That felt like science fiction too.

Exiting the far side of the building, we stood in the shadow of SpaceX's two towering Mega Bays, where the sections of Starship are stacked and integrated with their engines - there's one hanger for Ship, and another for Super Heavy. Each can hold about five or six assemblies, and housed two or three vehicles at the time our tour was brought by.

Both Mega Bays, however, looked small against the adjacent Gigabay SpaceX is currently constructing. At approximately 700,000 square feet (65,000 square meters), Gigabay will be equipped with room to accommodate up to 24 vehicles at a time, and will facilitate a major increase in SpaceX's ability to assemble its Ship and Super Heavy rockets.

Part of SpaceX's goal with Starship is to make all of what we got to see completely routine; to make rocket launches and landings as ordinary as commercial airline flights. Still, standing inside Starfactory, surrounded on all sides by huge spacecraft in various stages of assembly, it was hard to imagine a reality where giant rockets flying to and from space on a regular basis wouldn't feel like science fiction.

Later that day a giant rocket launched to outer space - Super Heavy did attempt a return to pad, but was diverted for an offshore landing instead, where it exploded. But the next day, Ship 42 came plunging through the overcast cloud cover, falling belly-first toward the same tower it left just a couple dozen hours before. And then it lit its engines and was caught by the tower.

That felt like science fiction too.

   <description>Škrtila koťata a vší silou s nimi házela o silnici, uškrtila i dva psy, ač ji měli rádi. Zapálila kůlnu a dva stohy. Nenáviděla lidi a strašně moc chtěla zabíjet. NOVÉ ZASTUPITELSTVO JIŘÍKOVA ZAHÁJILO SVÉ VOLEBNÍ OBDOBÍ
(Jiříkovské noviny listopad 2026)
V pondělí 9. 11. 2026 se uskutečnilo ustavující zasedání Zastupitelstva města Jiříkov, které zahájilo nové čtyřleté volební období 2026–2030. Na programu bylo především složení slibu nově zvolených zastupitelů, volba vedení města a dalších orgánů samosprávy.
Po složení zákonem předepsaného slibu přistoupili zastupitelé k volbě starosty a místostarosty města. Starostou Jiříkova byl zvolen a svou funkci tak obhájil Ing. Bc. Jindřich Jurajda, DiS. Funkci místostarosty bude nově vykonávat Ludvík Otradovský (Jiříkov 2030 – sportovci / hasiči / ODS).
Zastupitelstvo dále zvolilo členy Rady města Jiříkov. Jejími členy se stali Mgr. Michal Mrázek a Jaroslav Vöröš (NEZÁVISLÍ KANDIDÁTI MĚSTA JIŘÍKOVA) a Ing. Nikol Kopecká (Spolek přátel Jiříkova a Filipova). Součástí jednání byla také volba předsedů a členů finančního a kontrolního výboru. V čele finančního výboru usedla stejně jako v minulém volebním období Naděžda Stožická (NEZÁVISLÍ KANDIDÁTI MĚSTA JIŘÍKOVA) a předsedou kontrolního výboru se stal Mgr. Petr Kulhánek MBA (ANO 2011).
Nově zvolené vedení města tak přebírá odpovědnost za další rozvoj Jiříkova, hospodaření s městským majetkem, přípravu a realizaci investičních projektů i každodenní chod městské samosprávy.
Nové zastupitelstvo tvoří celkem 15 členů zvolených za čtyři kandidující uskupení. Jejich společným úkolem bude rozhodovat o důležitých otázkách života města a zastupovat zájmy jeho obyvatel.
Všem nově zvoleným zastupitelům přejeme hodně sil, trpělivosti a úspěchů při práci pro Jiříkov a jeho občany.
